nameStory: The "arrowfeather" name comes from the grass's distinctive seed heads, which split into three sharp, bristly points that look remarkably like the fletching feathers on an arrow. These three-pronged awns (the bristly extensions on grass seeds) give the entire threeawn genus its common name, but this species' particularly feathery appearance earned it the arrow comparison.
description: Arrowfeather threeawn is a native bunch grass that forms small clumps rather than spreading carpets. It typically grows 1-3 feet tall with narrow, wiry stems and thin leaves. The most distinctive feature is its seed head, which produces seeds with three slender, twisted bristles that catch the light and give the plant a delicate, almost ethereal appearance when backlit by the sun.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Each seed has exactly three long, thin bristles (awns) that are often twisted and can be up to 2 inches long, creating a feathery, almost spider-like appearance

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Very narrow, thread-like leaves that feel rough to the touch and roll inward, making them appear almost needle-like

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms tight bunches or tufts rather than spreading, with multiple stems arising from the base

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Wiry, slender stems that feel firm and slightly rough when you run your fingers along them

habitat: Look for arrowfeather threeawn in dry, sandy soils and open areas like fields, prairies, and woodland edges. In New England, it's most commonly found in disturbed sites, old fields, and areas with poor, well-drained soils where other grasses struggle to compete.

seasonality.spring: New green shoots emerge from the base, looking like thin grass blades. The plant is relatively inconspicuous at this stage.
seasonality.summer: Flowering occurs in mid to late summer, when the distinctive three-bristled seed heads begin to develop and become the plant's most noticeable feature.
seasonality.fall: Seeds mature and the three-pronged awns become most prominent, often catching autumn light beautifully. The plant may take on purplish tints.
seasonality.winter: Dried stems and old seed heads may persist, appearing as brittle, straw-colored tufts with some of the characteristic three-bristled seeds still attached.

funFact: The three bristles on each seed are actually tiny drill bits - they twist and turn with changes in humidity, literally screwing the seed into the ground for perfect planting depth without any help from animals or wind dispersal!
confusionNotes: Other threeawn grasses in the same genus all share the three-bristled seeds, but arrowfeather threeawn's bristles are typically the longest and most feathery-looking. If you see a grass with three bristles per seed, you've found a threeawn - then look at bristle length and overall plant size to narrow it down.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called "threeawn," don't confuse the awns with thorns or spines - they're actually modified parts of the flower that help with seed dispersal. The "purpurascens" in its scientific name hints at the purplish coloration the plant often develops.
compareHints: Arrowfeather threeawn is typically taller and more robust than most of its relatives like fork-tip three-awn, and its seed bristles are usually longer and more feathery than the shorter, stiffer bristles of oldfield three-awn. Seaside threeawn is restricted to coastal areas, while arrowfeather is found inland in various dry habitats.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the three-awn grasses in New England, Slim-spike has the most delicate, narrow flower spikes - much thinner than the more robust spikes of Arrowfeather Threeawn or the branched clusters of Fork-tip Three-awn.
Among its three-awn relatives in New England, Oldfield Three-awn is the most delicate and branched, with the most open, airy seed heads.
Among New England's three-awn grasses, fork-tip three-awn is unique for its distinctly forked branching pattern and smaller size.
Seaside Threeawn is distinguished from other New England threeawns primarily by its coastal habitat - it's the only species in the genus that grows directly in beach sand and tolerates salt spray.
Among New England's three-awn grasses, forked three-awn is distinguished by its branching pattern from the base rather than higher up the stem like fork-tip three-awn.
